title: The $3.1 million paid to fix the pipes under City Hall

beats.text: This case is an investigative lead. A steam leak damaged communications lines in 2020.

visual.sub: A leak prompted a competitively quoted emergency repair

beats.text: Public Works solicited quotes, even with emergency authority. The lowest responsive bidder won.

visual.kicker: A leak prompted a competitively quoted emergency repair

beats.text: In 2022, steam escaped from two manholes. One was directly in front of City Hall.

visual.kicker: Leaks returned and the City agreed to sell the loop for one dollar

beats.text: The City sold the loop for one dollar. The buyer took on future maintenance.

visual.kicker: Leaks returned and the City agreed to sell the loop for one dollar

beats.text: City staff estimated $4.9 million for immediate repairs.

visual.kicker: Leaks returned and the City agreed to sell the loop for one dollar

beats.text: Instead, the City paid the buyer $3.1 million upfront at closing.
We matched that payment to the signed agreement and the City’s voucher.

visual.kicker: The City paid the repair contribution at closing

beats.text: The repair schedule allowed three, six and nine months for the three phases.
The contract allowed extensions and set damages at $200 a day for qualifying delays.

visual.kicker: Three deadlines governed what the buyer had to deliver

beats.text: In January 2026, another steam leak notice appeared on the Larkin block.
The notice gives the block but no vault number.

visual.kicker: Later permits identify the blocks where crews returned

beats.text: The completion notices would show whether crews had finished the original work on time.
A lead is a question, not an accusation.
